title: The lapse rate: why the sky cools 6.5 K per kilometre, and the ladder that lifts the surface above the radiating level
intro: Every mountaineer knows the air gets colder going up, and every hot-air balloonist knows how sharply. The number, roughly 6.5 kelvin lost per kilometre climbed, held its ground long before anyone knew why the temperature should fall at all. The answer turns out to be thermodynamic, not radiative: a rising parcel of air expands as the pressure around it drops, does work against the surroundings, and cools without losing a single joule of heat to anything. That single mechanism sets the atmosphere's temperature ladder, fixes the altitude at which the planet radiates to space, and explains where the 33 K of surface warming we usually attribute to greenhouse gases actually comes from.

sections.heading: 1. Balloonists in the cold, and the wrong explanation

blocks.text: In August 1804, Joseph-Louis Gay-Lussac (a French chemist barely 26 years old) took off from the garden of the Conservatoire des Arts et Métiers in Paris in a hydrogen balloon. He carried a thermometer, a barometer, and a set of stoppered flasks. Six hours later he had climbed to 7016 metres, the highest any human had ever been, and the thermometer read −9.5 °C: the surface had been 30 °C. The drop, about 5.5 K per kilometre averaged over his climb, was the first honest number anyone had for how the atmosphere thinned with altitude. The stoppered flasks, opened at the top, later showed that the composition of the air was essentially unchanged: same 21 percent oxygen, same 78 percent nitrogen. Whatever was cooling the air, it was not that the air itself had changed.

The obvious explanation, the one every schoolchild reaches for, is that height means distance from the warm ground, and distance means less heat gets there. This picture is wrong in the specific way it needs to be wrong. Heat can travel from the ground upward by two mechanisms: conduction (which in still air is glacially slow, giving a fall-off length of a few centimetres, not kilometres) and radiation (which propagates at c and reaches the upper atmosphere in microseconds, so a warm ground would in fact heat the sky above it very quickly if that were the only account). Neither mechanism predicts a linear fall of 6.5 K/km through the entire troposphere (the lower layer of the atmosphere, the first 8-15 km above the surface). Something else has to be doing the cooling.

That something else is the vertical motion of air itself. Air rises in every thunderstorm, every warm afternoon over a sunlit field, every mountain updraft; it sinks over cold seas and inside high-pressure systems. Follow one parcel of air as it rises. It carries no thermometer, feels no external heat, and yet arrives at the top of its climb colder than it started. To see why, we need to work out what happens to a gas that is lifted into lower-pressure surroundings and forced to expand.

sections.heading: 2. The parcel argument: three steps to Γ = g/c_p

blocks.text: Imagine a small blob of air, big enough to have a well-defined temperature and pressure but small enough that it moves as one lump. Push it upward. The pressure around it, always set by the weight of the atmosphere above, drops as it climbs; and because the blob adjusts to match the surrounding pressure in a fraction of a second (much faster than it can exchange heat with the surrounding air by conduction), it expands. Expanding gases cool: this is the same effect that makes a bicycle pump valve go cold when you release the pressure. There is no external cooling; the parcel's internal energy is being spent on the work of pushing back the surrounding air. The whole argument turns on three separate physical statements, one about the gas, one about the atmosphere, and one about the connection.

First, the ideal-gas first law for an adiabatic process (adiabatic here meaning that the parcel exchanges no heat with its surroundings: dq = 0). For a rising parcel that matches the surrounding pressure at every instant, the relevant thermodynamic identity is that the change in enthalpy equals the volume times the change in pressure. Written per unit mass, and using the specific heat capacity at constant pressure c_p (the amount of heat, in joules per kilogram per kelvin, needed to raise the temperature of one kilogram of air by one kelvin while its pressure is held fixed), this reads out to the following relation between an infinitesimal temperature change dT and the corresponding infinitesimal pressure change dP.

blocks.caption: c_p is the specific heat capacity of air at constant pressure, about 1005 J/(kg·K) for dry air. dT is the infinitesimal temperature change of the parcel as it rises. dP is the infinitesimal pressure change the parcel experiences, always negative on the way up because pressure falls with altitude. ρ is the local mass density of the parcel, in kg/m³. The equation is the first law dU + P dV = 0 recast into enthalpy form dh = dP/ρ, valid for an adiabatic ideal-gas expansion.

blocks.text: Second, hydrostatic equilibrium. The pressure at any altitude in an atmosphere at rest is set by the weight of everything above. Push a slab of air up by dz and the pressure change is minus the density of the slab times g (Earth's gravitational acceleration, 9.81 m/s²) times dz. This is a mechanical statement about the surrounding atmosphere, not about the parcel.

blocks.caption: P is the atmospheric pressure at height z, in pascals. z is the altitude, in metres. ρ is the local air density, in kg/m³. g is the acceleration due to gravity, 9.81 m/s² near Earth's surface. The minus sign says pressure decreases with height because the column of air weighing down on a given level thins out as you climb.

blocks.text: Third, substitute one into the other. The parcel's pressure change dP matches the surrounding pressure change (that was the point of tracking a parcel that moves quietly through the atmosphere), so we can replace dP in the first equation with the −ρg dz from the second. The density ρ cancels on both sides, and what remains is the dry adiabatic lapse rate Γ_d: the fall in temperature per unit rise in altitude for a dry parcel.

blocks.caption: Γ_d is the dry adiabatic lapse rate, the temperature drop per kilometre of climb for a parcel of dry air, positive by convention because it measures a fall. g is the acceleration due to gravity, 9.81 m/s². c_p is the specific heat of dry air at constant pressure, 1005 J/(kg·K). The ratio is 9.76 × 10⁻³ K/m, or almost exactly 9.8 K/km, and the whole atmosphere-scale number has been derived from two constants of physics and one constant of the gas. There is no adjustable parameter.

quiz.question: Suppose Mars had an atmosphere identical to Earth's (same c_p ≈ 1005 J/(kg·K)) but subject to Mars's surface gravity of about 3.71 m/s². Roughly what would the dry adiabatic lapse rate be there?
options: About 9.8 K/km, the same as Earth
quiz.explanation: The formula Γ_d = g/c_p depends on g and c_p only. Change g from 9.81 to 3.71 (a factor of about 0.38) and the lapse rate scales by the same factor: 9.8 × 0.38 ≈ 3.7 K/km. Real Mars, with its very different atmospheric composition (mostly CO₂, with c_p ≈ 850 J/(kg·K)) and pervasive dust that alters radiative transfer, has an observed lapse of about 2.5 K/km on average, close to but slightly below this back-of-envelope value. Answer A ignores the derivation and assumes lapse is a universal property of atmospheres. Answer C multiplies by the wrong ratio, treating Mars's smaller g as if it should give a steeper lapse. Answer D uses Earth's g divided by Mars's g rather than the other way round, another common inversion. The right instinct is that a weaker pull of gravity means each metre of climb reveals a smaller drop in surrounding pressure, and therefore does less expansion work on the rising parcel.

sections.heading: 3. The wet lapse and the 6.5 K/km compromise

blocks.text: The 9.8 K/km of the dry adiabatic argument is not what the atmosphere shows. Balloon and radiosonde measurements (radiosondes being the small instrument packages carried aloft twice a day from thousands of weather stations since the 1930s, sending back temperature and humidity by radio) consistently report an average of about 6.5 K/km through the troposphere. Between the honest derivation and the observed number sits water vapour, and it is what closes the gap.

A real air parcel is not dry. It carries humidity, typically a few grams of water vapour per kilogram of air. As the parcel rises and cools, it eventually reaches its dew point, the temperature at which the vapour is saturated and further cooling forces water molecules out of the gas phase and into liquid droplets. Every gram of water that condenses releases about 2.5 megajoules per kilogram of latent heat (the energy that was stored in the freedom of the vapour molecules and is given up when they lock into a liquid). That heat goes straight back into the parcel and partially offsets the cooling from expansion. The result is the moist adiabatic lapse rate Γ_m, which depends on temperature (warmer parcels can hold more vapour and release more latent heat) but averages around 5 K/km in the lower troposphere.

blocks.caption: Interactive parcel ascent. Drag the surface temperature slider (255 to 305 K) and the surface relative humidity slider (0 to 100 percent) to see how a rising parcel of air cools with altitude. Two curves are drawn: the dry adiabatic line at 9.8 K/km all the way up, and the actual parcel path (dry adiabatic below the lifting condensation level, moist adiabatic above it). The observed environmental average 6.5 K/km is drawn as a dashed reference.

blocks.text: The atmosphere at large is neither dry nor perfectly moist. It is a stew: dry over deserts, saturated over rain forests, mixed by turbulence and by the passage of weather systems that overturn air across latitudes. The 6.5 K/km figure was fixed by international convention in 1962 (in the U.S. Standard Atmosphere, a table of temperature and pressure versus altitude adopted for aviation and rocketry calibration) as the average tropospheric lapse rate over the mid-latitudes. That number sits, not by coincidence, between the 9.8 K/km of a dry parcel and the roughly 5 K/km of a saturated one, weighted toward the moist end because most of the atmosphere's mass, and most of its weather, sits over ocean. The observed 6.5 K/km is not a fundamental constant; it is what the planet's actual mix of water and turbulence averages to. On a bone-dry desert dawn the local lapse can climb close to the dry adiabat; on a saturated maritime tropical day it can drop to the wet value.

sections.heading: 4. The radiating level, and where 33 K of greenhouse warming lives

blocks.text: The temperature ladder built by the lapse rate is more than an atmospheric curiosity: it is the mechanism by which the greenhouse effect actually turns into surface warming. To see this, recall the planetary equilibrium temperature T_eff, the temperature at which a blackbody balances the absorbed sunlight against the emitted infrared (about 255 K for Earth, from σT_eff⁴ times four times the planet's cross-sectional area equal to the absorbed solar flux). The surface, however, sits at a global average of 288 K. The 33 K gap is the greenhouse effect, but stated this way it is not yet a mechanism: it is a discrepancy.

The mechanism appears when you ask where in the atmosphere the outgoing infrared radiation actually leaves for space. Because water vapour and carbon dioxide absorb thermal infrared strongly, an infrared photon emitted from the surface almost never makes it to space directly; it is absorbed, re-emitted, absorbed again, in a random walk that continues until the photon finds itself in air thin enough that it can escape. The altitude at which that escape becomes typical is called the effective radiating level, or radiating height, z_R, and for present-day Earth it sits around 5 km up in the mid-troposphere. It is the layer of atmosphere that acts, when seen from space, as the planet's radiating skin.

The radiating level is at T_eff = 255 K by definition (that is what it means to radiate as a blackbody in balance with the absorbed sunlight). The surface is connected to it by the ladder of the lapse rate. Multiply the two numbers together and the 33 K is not a mysterious greenhouse bonus; it is a bookkeeping consequence of z_R sitting above the surface by exactly the amount the lapse rate says it does.

blocks.caption: T_surface is the average surface air temperature, about 288 K for Earth. T_eff is the planetary effective temperature at the radiating level, about 255 K for Earth, set by the balance between absorbed sunlight and emitted infrared. Γ is the environmental lapse rate, about 6.5 K/km. z_R is the effective radiating height, the altitude at which the planet's infrared emission actually escapes to space, about 5 km for present-day Earth. The equation says the greenhouse warming at the surface is the product of the lapse rate and the height difference to the radiating level; more opacity pushes z_R up, and the same Γ then delivers a larger surface warming.

blocks.text: This is why climate sensitivity turns on where the radiating level sits. Add carbon dioxide to the atmosphere and the infrared opacity climbs. The photon random walk has to go further before it finds thin air, so z_R rises. Because the lapse rate above z_R is still Γ, the new radiating level is colder than the old one (colder by Γ times the height increase). If the same solar input has to be radiated to space at a colder temperature, that is a violation of energy balance, and the planet responds by warming: everything, including z_R, is pushed up in temperature until the new z_R reaches 255 K again. The surface, sitting Γ · z_R below, warms by exactly the same amount. The greenhouse effect is not, at bottom, about a blanket absorbing heat. It is about how far up the atmosphere pushes its own emitting surface.

quiz.question: Suppose adding CO₂ to Earth's atmosphere raises the effective radiating height z_R from 5.0 km to 5.5 km, without changing the environmental lapse rate Γ = 6.5 K/km. What is the resulting change in surface temperature at equilibrium?
options: No change: T_eff is set by the sunlight balance and does not respond to CO₂
quiz.explanation: Use T_surface = T_eff + Γ · z_R. T_eff at the new radiating level is still 255 K (the balance with absorbed sunlight is unchanged, by the same solar constant and albedo). The lapse rate is unchanged at 6.5 K/km. The height change is 0.5 km. Multiply: 6.5 × 0.5 = 3.25 K, so the surface warms by about 3.3 K. Answer A gets the sign right for the new radiating layer (that layer does cool, in the sense that the old air at 5 km used to be 255 K and now it is Γ · 0.5 = 3.3 K colder because the whole profile has slid up) but confuses the layer's cooling with the surface's response. Answer B misses the entire point of the mechanism: T_eff is set by sunlight balance, but the level at which T_eff is realized moves, and the surface moves with it. Answer D is the full present-day greenhouse effect (33 K) rather than the change from a small CO₂ increment, and would require pushing z_R all the way up by 5 km, which no realistic forcing does. The take-home is that surface warming, in this picture, is simply the lapse rate times the rise of the radiating level.

sections.heading: 5. Standard atmospheres and the stratosphere's turn upward

blocks.text: The 1962 U.S. Standard Atmosphere is a table of pressure, temperature, and density from sea level up to 80 km, calibrated to match mid-latitude annual averages measured by weather balloons over the previous decade. It sets Γ = 6.5 K/km from the surface up to 11 km, which is where it draws the tropopause (the boundary between the troposphere, where the lapse rate we have been discussing dominates, and the layer above). From 11 to 20 km it makes the temperature constant at 216.65 K. From 20 to 47 km it makes the temperature climb, actually climb, at a rate of about 3 K/km. The atmosphere has stopped cooling with altitude and started warming with it. That reversal is not a rounding error in the table; it is a real feature of the sky, and it is the fingerprint of ozone.

Ozone (O₃, the triatomic form of oxygen) absorbs solar ultraviolet in the 200 to 300 nanometre band, the same absorption that shields the biosphere from UV-B damage. Most of the atmosphere's ozone sits in a layer between 15 and 35 km up, produced there by photolysis of O₂ by even shorter-wavelength UV. Every joule of solar UV absorbed by ozone becomes heat, deposited exactly at the altitude where the absorption happens. That local heat source overturns the sign of the temperature gradient: the layer is being warmed from within by the Sun rather than cooled by adiabatic ascent from below, and the temperature climbs with altitude accordingly. The stratosphere is not a layer where the parcel argument stops applying; it is a layer where a competing heat source, absorbed UV, drowns out the adiabatic cooling.

This is the deep lesson buried in a boring aviation table. The shape of the atmospheric temperature profile at any altitude is a diagnostic of what heating and cooling processes dominate there. In the troposphere, adiabatic ascent from a warm surface dominates, and the temperature falls at 6.5 K/km. At the tropopause, adiabatic cooling and radiative cooling balance and the temperature holds flat. In the stratosphere, ozone UV absorption dominates and the temperature climbs. Higher up, in the mesosphere (50 to 85 km) the ozone runs out, adiabatic cooling wins again, and the temperature falls to the coldest point in the whole vertical column, near 180 K at the mesopause. Every kink in the profile is a story about which physics is doing the arithmetic at that altitude, and the parcel argument of section 2 is one of the two or three most powerful stories in the whole column.

finalQuiz.question: A weather balloon over the mid-Pacific in a saturated tropical air mass measures a local lapse rate of about 5 K/km through the lower troposphere, well below the 6.5 K/km of the U.S. Standard Atmosphere and clearly below the dry adiabatic 9.8 K/km. Which of the following is the correct read?
options: The measurement is wrong: the dry adiabatic derivation Γ_d = g/c_p is a theorem, and no honest lapse can fall below it
The air mass is well above the dew point, so no condensation is happening; the measured 5 K/km must be a radiative-cooling artifact rather than a real thermodynamic profile

The parcel is saturated and rising: condensation is releasing latent heat as the parcel cools, partially offsetting the adiabatic expansion, and driving the observed lapse toward the moist adiabatic value of about 5 K/km
The tropopause has descended below the balloon, so the balloon is sampling the isothermal lower stratosphere, which is why the lapse rate has fallen
finalQuiz.explanation: Saturated tropical air is exactly the regime in which the moist adiabatic lapse Γ_m applies, and Γ_m ≈ 5 K/km through the lower troposphere is precisely what section 3 predicts. Every gram of water condensing during ascent releases about 2.5 MJ/kg of latent heat back into the parcel, partially compensating the adiabatic cooling from expansion and dropping the effective lapse rate below Γ_d = g/c_p. Answer A misreads the dry adiabatic derivation as an inequality: it is a theorem about a dry parcel, and a moist parcel that is condensing has an extra heat source not included in the derivation, so it lapses less steeply. Answer B has the physics backwards: it is the condensation itself, occurring because the parcel is saturated, that reduces the lapse; unsaturated parcels lapse at Γ_d. Answer D confuses altitude ranges: the isothermal stratosphere begins at 11 km in the mid-latitudes, higher over the tropics (up to 17 km), and a lower-tropospheric balloon measurement over the ocean is nowhere near it. The 5 K/km reading in this scenario is a textbook signature of the wet-adiabatic mechanism, and it is why global average Γ sits around 6.5 K/km rather than at either dry or moist extreme.
